conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional changes that can happen after a baby arrives. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. My goal is to create a warm, safe space where you can speak openly, so we can figure out together what kind of support might be most helpful for you right now.

We’ll move through the questions at your pace; each one focuses on a different aspect of mood, anxiety, and coping since your baby was born. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start, could you tell me:  
In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has that been happening as much as it used to, less often, or not at all?
Um… definitely not as much. I can still laugh sometimes—like if my husband shows me a funny video—but it feels kind of forced, and it doesn’t last. Most of the time I’m too tired or just… down.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, just not the way I used to. It feels kind of distant, like I’m faking it more often than not.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like when my mom offers to come over or when I get a quiet moment to drink my coffee—but mostly I just feel flat. When the day starts, I don’t think “oh, this will be nice”; I just wonder how I’ll make it through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to a check-up, I’ll replay in my head and tell myself a better mom would’ve handled it. It’s not every second of the day, but it’s definitely been happening most days this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my chest feels tight, worrying that his breathing sounds different or that I didn’t sanitize the pacifier well enough. I know in my head it’s probably fine, but the thoughts just keep looping and I can’t shut them off. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… maybe two or three times this week. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t breathe. Nothing’s happening—baby’s asleep, the house is quiet—but it feels like something awful is about to happen. It passes if I walk around and drink water, but in the moment it’s scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. It feels like the second I finish one thing—changing a diaper, washing bottles—there’s already another mess or cry waiting. I keep a little checklist in my head and it never gets fully checked off, so I end the day feeling like I failed even though I barely sat down.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I’m just lying there staring at the ceiling. My mind keeps running through everything I might’ve messed up or all the “what-ifs” about him getting sick. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and even when I do I wake up with a jolt, sure I heard him cry.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this grey cloud hanging over me. I’ll look at the baby and feel guilty that I’m not happier—he’s healthy, I’m supposed to be grateful—but the sadness just sits there. Some hours are a little better, but it never fully lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t nap and I just felt like I was failing him; I ended up sobbing in the rocker. Another night my partner asked how my day was and I just burst into tears for no real reason. It’s not all day long, but when it hits I can’t stop the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Um… maybe once or twice. It was more like a quick, scary picture—what if I just kept driving past the house instead of turning in, or what if I didn’t wake up. I don’t want to die, and I’d never leave my baby, but the thought popped in and freaked me out. I don’t have any plan or anything like that.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a constant heaviness and worry. Laughing now feels distant, and even small pleasures like coffee or visits don't lift the grey cloud that arrives with you each morning. You're exhausted yet unable to sleep, replaying mistakes and fears about your baby's safety, and you blame yourself whenever anything goes wrong. Moments of panic and tears catch you off guard, and fleeting scary thoughts have popped in-though you quickly emphasize you would never act on them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to enjoy laughter, describing it as distant and fake—semantically aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent anhedonia ('feel flat') and absence of anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "a lot" and "most days this week," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without clear cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected episodes of intense fear and physical panic symptoms occurring multiple times this week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" and unable to complete tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating sleep due to racing anxious thoughts and frequent awakening, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness with pervasive guilt and only partial relief, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear tearful episodes twice this week triggered by perceived failure and unexplained sadness, mapping to "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total ≥14 (here 25) indicates probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your answers meet core DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day (<quote>pretty much every day</quote>), diminished interest (<quote>feel flat</quote>), guilt (<quote>I'm doing something wrong</quote>), concentration trouble, and recurrent thoughts of death. Daily anxiety and panic episodes also suggest comorbid <med>perinatal anxiety disorder</medi>. Item-10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Call 988 or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Share these results with your partner or support person so they can help monitor mood and safety
4. Begin gentle daily structure: short outdoor walks, balanced meals, hydration-set a 20-minute timer so tasks feel less overwhelming
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when panic rises: inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s; repeat x4
6. Limit evening screen time; try a warm shower and lavender scent to cue sleep after night feeds
7. Accept help with night shifts or household chores; rest is protective for mood and milk supply
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after treatment starts
9. Explore local support groups or online communities for new moms with <med>postpartum depression</med>
10. Bring baby's pediatrician into the loop; they can provide extra parenting confidence and resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary (not diagnostic)

Presenting symptoms:
- Persistent low mood, “grey cloud,” daily sadness, frequent tearfulness
- Marked anhedonia: reports feeling “flat,” unable to anticipate or feel enjoyment
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care; rumination over perceived failures
- Daily, intrusive anxiety/worry (health of baby, competence as mother) with physical tension
- Two to three sudden panic-like episodes this week (racing heart, breathlessness) without clear trigger
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to racing thoughts; wakes “with a jolt”
- Sense of being overwhelmed most of the time; tasks feel unmanageable
- Diminished concentration and pleasure in previously enjoyable activities
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting thoughts of not waking up, driving past house) without intent or plan; patient reports these thoughts “freaked me out”

Pattern:
Consistent with significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; functional impact evident in sleep disruption, coping, and emotional bonding.

Screening significance:
High endorsement of core mood, anxiety, guilt, and coping items; safety concern due to presence of self-harm images, albeit no active plan or intent.

Risk factors noted:
- Daily dysphoria, anhedonia, guilt
- Insomnia secondary to mood
- Recurrent panic-tinged anxiety
- Passive suicidal ideation (safety flag)

Overall screening impression:
Patient scores in high-risk range for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment recommended; consider expedited referral for comprehensive perinatal mental-health evaluation and support.
